analysis.subject: civics
analysis.pageCoverage: The page covers the Article V basis for amending the Constitution, the two proposal methods, the joint resolution route without a presidential role, transmission to governors and state legislatures, and examination and certification of ratifications.

overview.headline: How amendments are proposed, sent to states, and ratified

keyPoints.point: Students learn that the Constitution provides that an amendment may be proposed by Congress with a two-thirds vote or by a convention.
keyPoints.quote: The Constitution provides that an amendment may be proposed either by the Congress with a two-thirds majority vote

keyPoints.point: Students learn that the President has no constitutional role in the amendment process and does not sign the joint resolution.
keyPoints.quote: Since the President does not have a constitutional role in the amendment process

keyPoints.point: Students learn that the Archivist submits the proposed amendment to each Governor for consideration by the states.
keyPoints.quote: The Archivist submits the proposed amendment to the States for their consideration by sending a letter of notification to each Governor

keyPoints.point: Students learn that a proposed amendment becomes part of the Constitution when ratified by three-fourths of the states.
keyPoints.quote: A proposed amendment becomes part of the Constitution as soon as it is ratified by three-fourths of the States (38 of 50 States).

keyTerms.gloss: Constitutional provision that authorizes the amendment authority and process
keyTerms.quote: The authority to amend the Constitution of the United States is derived from Article V of the Constitution.

keyTerms.gloss: Legislative form Congress uses to propose an amendment
keyTerms.quote: The Congress proposes an amendment in the form of a joint resolution.

keyTerms.gloss: Official who submits the proposed amendment to governors and later certifies ratification
keyTerms.quote: The Archivist submits the proposed amendment to the States for their consideration by sending a letter of notification to each Governor

keyTerms.gloss: Review of ratification documents for legal sufficiency before acknowledgment
keyTerms.quote: The OFR examines ratification documents for facial legal sufficiency and an authenticating signature.

keyTerms.gloss: Required share of states that must ratify for an amendment to be adopted
keyTerms.quote: A proposed amendment becomes part of the Constitution as soon as it is ratified by three-fourths of the States (38 of 50 States).

componentPlan.pedagogicalReason: Shows the ordered workflow from congressional proposal through state consideration to final certification.
componentPlan.focusQuote: The Constitution provides that an amendment may be proposed either by the Congress with a two-thirds majority vote

componentPlan.pedagogicalReason: Makes the three-fourths requirement concrete by showing 38 of 50 states as the adoption point.
componentPlan.focusQuote: A proposed amendment becomes part of the Constitution as soon as it is ratified by three-fourths of the States (38 of 50 States).
